newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FARM UNION SAYS WILL DENY HUNGARY HUF80BLN IN TAX.
newsitem.headline: FARM UNION SAYS WILL DENY HUNGARY HUF80BLN IN TAX.

text.p: Hungary's biggest farm cooperatives union MOSZ on Tuesday announced it would encourage its members to register as individual farmers, thus denying the government tens of billions of forints in tax revenues.
"It could be as high as 80 billion forints," MOSZ's president Tamas Nagy told reporters following a union meeting.

The move follows a government decision last month to grant tax relief to private farmers as a concession to a fringe farmers union, METESZ, which blocked roads throughout Hungary in protest at new tax rules.
"The government has clearly indicated by this that it is only prepared to bow to pressure, instead of reasonable negotiations," Nagy said.
A February demonstration in the central Hungarian town of Kiskoros sparked a series of farmers' protests following 1997 income and social security tax increases for individual farmers.
The government made a series of initial concessions, since passed into law, to the farmers, who have since formed METESZ.
Government officials said at the time the concessions would not result in a significant tax or social security income loss for the budget.
MOSZ officials said that they expect about half of their 150,000 members to become individual farmers by the end of the year but this would not mean giving up cooperatives altogether.
"This would only be a change in accounting techniques, and that can be done in a few weeks," Nagy said.
Another MOSZ official said all the benefits of collective farming would still be available to farmers who choose to register as individual producers for tax reasons.
"It would be fully serviced individual farming," said Gabor Horvath, MOSZ general secretary.

He also said the government's recently announced ten-year farming policy draft was little more than an overview of the present situation combined with a "wishlist" containing no concrete solution to existing problems.

Hungary's agricultural output has dropped some 40 percent since the mid-80s and the Socialist-led government, which came to power in the summer of 1994, first presented a long-term farming policy draft at the beginning of March.
The government plans to finalise the document by the end of April and eventually turn it into a farming law.
Horvath said the government should instead identify and solve the seven or eight most pressing problems and leave more time to reach a compromise on a long-term policy.
MOSZ opposes the government's stance, included in the farming policy draft, to maintain a ban on farmland ownership by companies.
Union leaders said they regarded protests as a last resort, but did not rule out action if the government was not prepared for meaningful talks.
"Half of the board members were in favour of some sort of action and the atmosphere was very tense," Nagy said.
